report.source_text: This patient was admitted to hospital and acyclovir 1.8 g daily by intravenous infusion was provided followed by oral valacyclovir 3 g per day. She received an intravitreal forscarnet injection (1.2 mg/0.05 mL). Close liaison was undertaken with clinical microbiology and genitourinary medicine. The HIV-positive result was discussed with the patient and antiretroviral therapy (ART) commenced.

report.source_text: Following 1 week of ART, a repeat serum VZV DNA test was negative. Vision remains at NPL in both eyes. Bilateral RDs were considered as inoperable. The patient was registered blind and has had input from social services and community occupational therapy including modifications to her home because of acquired visual loss.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A retired woman with long-standing unrecognized HIV infection (CD4 37 cells/µL, viral load 116,912 copies/mL) presented with a 4-week history of progressive right vision loss. She had a documented 18-month history of left herpes zoster ophthalmicus and 7-month keratouveitis. On examination, the right eye showed vitreous haze, multiple areas of white retinal swelling in the posterior pole with macular involvement, and obliterated arterioles with perivascular sheathing (Kyrieleis' plaques). Bilateral retinal detachments were confirmed on ultrasound. Aqueous humor PCR from anterior chamber paracentesis was positive for varicella-zoster virus (VZV) DNA and negative for CMV and HSV. Serology confirmed HIV positivity and varicella-zoster IgG positivity, with negative CMV and Toxoplasma serology. The patient was treated with intravenous acyclovir 1.8 g daily followed by oral valacyclovir 3 g per day, intravitreal foscarnet injection (1.2 mg/0.05 mL), and antiretroviral therapy was initiated. One week after ART initiation, serum VZV DNA became negative. However, vision remained at no perception of light in both eyes, bilateral retinal detachments were deemed inoperable, and the patient was registered blind.
